title: Building an HTTP Server
summary: Create a web server with node:http, inspect requests, send status codes, headers and JSON, route by method and path, and read a POST body with no framework at all.
introduction: Node ships a complete HTTP server in the `node:http` module; Express and every other framework is a layer on top of it. Writing a small server by hand first means you will always know what those frameworks are doing for you: parsing the URL, reading the body, setting headers and finishing the response. In this lesson you build a tiny book API with nothing but the core module, test it with curl, and learn the one rule that explains most hanging requests: every response must be ended.
learningObjectives: Start a server with createServer and listen and test it with curl
Read the method, URL and headers of a request and send status codes, headers and JSON
Route requests by method and path and read a JSON request body

blocks.text: `createServer` takes a function that Node calls once per request with two objects: `req`, a readable stream describing the incoming request, and `res`, a writable stream for your reply. `listen` binds a port and starts accepting connections; the process keeps running until you stop it with Ctrl+C.

blocks.title: server.js

blocks.text: Run `node server.js` in one terminal and talk to it from a second one with `curl`. The `-i` flag prints the response headers as well as the body:

blocks.title: Terminal (the Date header shows the moment of the request)
blocks.content:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/plain
Date: Sun, 15 Nov 2026 10:12:08 GMT
Connection: keep-alive
Keep-Alive: timeout=5
Content-Length: 19

Hello from Node.js

blocks.text: You wrote one header; Node added the rest. `Date` is required by the HTTP specification, `Connection` and `Keep-Alive` let the client reuse the connection for its next request, and `Content-Length` was computed from the string passed to `end`. Opening `http://localhost:3000` in a browser shows the same text.

blocks.title: curl on Windows
blocks.text: In Windows PowerShell 5, `curl` is an alias for `Invoke-WebRequest`, which has different flags. Type `curl.exe` instead, or run the examples in Git Bash or WSL, where the quoting used in this tutorial works unchanged.
What a request and a response contain

rows: `'GET'`, `'POST'`, `'PUT'`, `'DELETE'` and so on, always upper case
Path and query string as sent by the client, for example `'/api/books?q=dune'`; it does not include the host
An object with lower-case header names: `req.headers['content-type']`
Set the status and headers one at a time before anything is written
Set status and several headers in one call
Send part of the body; the response stays open
Send the last chunk (if any) and finish the response. Required for every request

blocks.title: The request that never finishes
blocks.text: If a code path forgets `res.end()`, the client waits forever: no error, no log line, just a spinner until it gives up. Every branch of your handler, including error branches, must end the response exactly once. Sending a second response is the mirror-image bug: `writeHead` after the headers have gone out throws `ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT`, so `return` as soon as you have sent a response.

`req.url` is just a string, so parse it with the standard `URL` class. The second argument supplies a base, because `req.url` has no host. The resulting object gives you `pathname` and `searchParams` separately. With that, routing is an `if` chain over method and path, and a small helper keeps the JSON responses consistent:

blocks.title: api.js

blocks.code:
curl -s "http://localhost:3000/api/books?q=neu"
curl -s -X POST -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"title":"Snow Crash"}' http://localhost:3000/api/books
curl -s http://localhost:3000/nope

items: `-s` silences curl's progress meter, `-X` sets the method, `-H` adds a header and `-d` sends a body.
Query parameters come back as strings or `null`; `searchParams.get('q')?.toLowerCase()` copes with a missing `q`.
Each `return` after `sendJson` guarantees that exactly one response goes out per request.
`201 Created` is the right status for a successful POST that made a new resource; `400 Bad Request` for input the client can fix; `404 Not Found` for an unknown route.

blocks.text: The body is not parsed for you and does not arrive in one piece. Because `req` is a readable stream (see the [previous lesson](/tutorials/nodejs/events-streams)), `for await (const chunk of req)` collects it chunk by chunk; the loop ends when the client has sent everything. `readJsonBody` then parses the text, and the `try`/`catch` around it turns malformed JSON into a `400` instead of a crash. The handler is `async` only so that it can `await` the body; Node does not care what the handler returns.

blocks.title: Restarting during development
blocks.text: Changing `api.js` does not affect the running server. Start it with `node --watch api.js` and Node restarts it automatically whenever a file it loaded changes. If a restart fails with `EADDRINUSE: address already in use`, an older copy is still holding port 3000: stop it with Ctrl+C.

You now have everything a framework provides, written by hand: routing, JSON responses, body parsing and status codes. It took about forty lines for two routes, and the `if` chain grows with every endpoint. The next lesson introduces [Express](/tutorials/nodejs/express-basics), which packages exactly these patterns into a few method calls.

questions.question: A handler sets `res.statusCode = 404` and a header but the client keeps waiting. What is missing?
questions.explanation: Setting the status and headers does not send anything; the response is only sent and finished when res.end() is called.

questions.question: To split `req.url` into a path and query parameters, create `new ___(req.url, 'http://localhost')`.
questions.explanation: The standard URL class parses the path and query string; the base argument is needed because req.url contains no host.
